result.source_concept: Packing a suitcase by tossing items in without regard to order, while counting each type of item

mappings.source_element: individual clothing items (e.g., t‑shirts, jeans, jackets)
mappings.relation: corresponds to the basic units being represented

mappings.source_element: lack of concern for the order in which items are placed in the suitcase
mappings.target_element: ignoring word order and grammar in the document representation
mappings.evidence: Analogy says "you don't care about the order" just as bag‑of‑words ignores word order

mappings.source_element: count of each clothing type (e.g., 5 t‑shirts)
mappings.relation: both retain quantitative information about each element
mappings.evidence: Analogy notes "you do keep track of how many of each item you packed" analogous to word frequencies

mappings.source_element: the suitcase as a collection of items
mappings.target_element: the document as an unordered multiset of words
mappings.evidence: Analogy equates "the suitcase (the document) is now just a collection of items (words) with their quantities"

result.process_summary: Both the suitcase‑packing scenario and the bag‑of‑words model represent a whole (document/suitcase) as an unordered collection of basic elements (words/clothing items) where the only retained information is the count of each element, discarding any ordering or structural relationships.
potential_breaks: The suitcase analogy introduces a physical space limitation (capacity of the suitcase) that has no counterpart in the abstract bag‑of‑words representation.
Treating items as completely independent may understate that bag‑of‑words also ignores semantic relationships between words, a limitation not explicitly highlighted by the analogy.
